reject_reason: other: invalid evidence - the README speed and LZ4/Zstd/ZIP comparison table has no measurement behind it and is contradicted by the repo's own benchmark output and code
tier_reason: README.txt lists NZ1 2.8/4.2 GB/s against LZ4 0.7/5 GB/s, Zstd 0.5/1.5 GB/s and ZIP 0.12/0.25 GB/s, but the repo contains no code that runs LZ4, Zstd or zlib, no dataset, CPU or flags; the only measured numbers (tests.txt, produced by the main() in nz1.c) are 29.31 MB/s compress and 30.99 MB/s decompress on a 1 MiB repeating alphabet, roughly 100x below the README claim. With no measured comparison against any baseline the record cannot sit above D.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README.txt only (no measurement code for it): NZ1 ~58% ratio, 2.8 GB/s compress, 4.2 GB/s decompress on x86 AVX2 (1.9/3.1 GB/s NEON, 0.8/1.5 GB/s scalar); comparison table lists LZ4 ~80%, 0.7 GB/s, 5 GB/s; Zstd ~60%, 0.5 GB/s, 1.5 GB/s; ZIP ~65%, 0.12 GB/s, 0.25 GB/s. The repo's own tests.txt (output of nz1.c main) shows 29.31 MB/s compress and 30.99 MB/s decompress on 1 MiB of repeating 'A'-'Z' (1.55% ratio) and 29.23/30.98 MB/s on 1 MiB of i%256 bytes, hardware not stated.
corrections.workload: README: none stated. nz1.c benchmark(): one clock()-timed run each on synthetic inputs (100 B 'ABCDE' repeat, 500 B lorem ipsum, 1 MiB repeating alphabet, 1 MiB i%256 ramp, 64 B fixed binary); no real corpus, no baseline library runs.
corrections.caveats: No benchmark against LZ4, Zstd or zlib exists in the repo; the comparison rows are unmeasured and implausible (LZ4 at an 80% ratio, worse than ZIP, is not a normal LZ4 result). The repo's own tests.txt shows ~29-31 MB/s, about 100x below the README's 2.8/4.2 GB/s, and the output ends with '[Program finished]' (an Android IDE/terminal banner), so hardware is unknown. Both nanozip_compress and nanozip_decompress run a bit-at-a-time CRC32 (8 dependent shift/xor steps per byte) over the whole buffer, so the code cannot plausibly reach GB/s rates as written. Format is byte-aligned LZ77 (4-byte match tokens, 0xBF-escaped literals >= 0xBF, no entropy coding), so the ~58% ratio claim versus LZ4 is unsupported. README says the window is configurable 1 KB to 1 MB, but nz1.c caps it at 65535 bytes (MAX_WINDOW). The x86 SIMD compare uses (1 << SIMD_WIDTH) - 1 with SIMD_WIDTH 32, which is undefined behaviour on int; AVX2 intrinsics are used unconditionally on x86_64. Unlike stb-zip, the CRC32 here is the standard reflected 0xEDB88320 CRC and the decoder checks it, so round-trip correctness on the shipped tests looks sound. Same author as stb-zip.

notes: Read nz1.c (586 lines) and tests.txt: the only real measurement is the author's own 29-31 MB/s run, and nothing in the repo times LZ4/Zstd/ZIP, so the README comparison table is invalid evidence in the same family as the stb-zip precedent. If the orchestrator keeps it under keep-and-document, it belongs at tier D with the caveats above. Metadata checked: MIT, 35 stars, 4 forks, 7 commits, last commit 2025-08-26 (stale), not a fork.

tier_reason: Upgraded C to B: the README cites the peer-reviewed paper (Kerbiriou and Chikhi, HiCOMB 2019 workshop, IPDPSW 2019, pp. 209-217, doi 10.1109/IPDPSW.2019.00042), whose Table II shows gunzip 37, libdeflate 118 and pugz (32 threads) 611 MB/s on a 2x12-core Xeon E5-2670 v3. Not A: the README benchmark script (example/bigger_benchmark.sh), Makefile flags and CPU models are public, but the compiler and version are not stated (Makefile uses $(CXX)).

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Makefile: -std=c++11 -mssse3 -O3 -flto -march=native -mtune=native -g; 'make asserts=0' adds -DNDEBUG (README recommends it for maximal performance). Compiler ($(CXX)) and version not stated.
corrections.caveats: Prototype: may crash, or give undefined behaviour with asserts=0; blocked/multi-part gzip files and non-ASCII (binary) data are unsupported. pugz skips CRC32 verification while gunzip computes it (README: CRC would cost roughly 33%), so the comparison is not equal work. Paper speeds come from files preloaded in memory with output sent unsynchronized to /dev/null (order-insensitive, mimicking a FASTQ parser); the README 'full decompression' column keeps ordered output and scales far less (251 MB/s at 24 threads vs 1052 MB/s line counting). README speeds are compressed-input bytes per second from a wall-clock shell script (example/bigger_benchmark.sh, divides by 1024*1024) on HIGGS.csv.gz and SRR6832872.fastq.gz. Compiler and version not stated. GitHub fork of ebiggers/libdeflate. The newer rapidgzip (already catalogued) covers the general case.

notes: All README and paper Table II numbers match the record; the paper does name its venue via the README citation (HiCOMB/IPDPSW 2019), so peer-review credit applies and the tier rises to B. Metadata checked: MIT, 124 stars, 11 forks, 88 commits, last commit 2019-08-20 (abandoned), GitHub fork of ebiggers/libdeflate.
